_meta.interpretation: K-means splits them into the three groups it was asked for: a large younger group, an older group on a similar typical income, and a small group whose average income is roughly three times the others'. Read that as a convenient split rather than a discovery. The younger and older groups look like two halves of one continuous age range cut near the middle, and the high-income group is the long upper tail of incomes rather than a separate population. The algorithm always returns as many groups as you ask for, whether or not the data has them; check the share of the spread the groups explain in the grouper's components (the full preset shows them), try a different number of groups, and ask what each group means for a decision before naming segments. Age and income are standardised first, so both count equally despite their different units.
_meta.question: Do customers fall into natural groups by age and income?
_meta.description: Segment customers.pulse into three clusters by age and income with GROUP_KMEANS: seeded k-means++ starts then Lloyd on z-scored members, keys cluster_1..cluster_3 by descending size (key column GROUP_KMEANS_age). Each cluster reports its size and mean age and income; Components carry the centroids, within-SS and the between-SS ratio. Same data and seed always give the same labels.
